title: Arjuna's Crisis and the Undying Self
intro: Chapters 1 and 2 of the Bhagavad Gita: Arjuna's despair on the battlefield and Krishna's first teaching on the self that never dies.

posts.caption: The Bhagavad Gita, "the Song of the Lord," is a 700-verse dialogue within India's great epic, the Mahabharata. It opens with the blind king Dhritarashtra asking Sanjaya, who has been granted divine sight, what is happening on the battlefield of Kurukshetra; the whole Gita is Sanjaya's answer. Many commentators hear a family already divided in the king's "my people and the Pandavas," his own nephews. Here, the Gita in order, one verse a day, beginning with 46 days on chapters 1 and 2.

posts.display: My limbs fail and my mouth is parched, my body quivers, and my hair stands on end.
posts.caption: The Gita's teaching begins with a human breakdown. Two branches of one family face each other: the Kauravas, the blind king's sons, and their cousins the Pandavas. Arjuna, the great Pandava archer, has asked his friend and charioteer Krishna to drive between the armies. There he sees uncles, teachers, cousins and friends ready to fight, and his body gives way. All that Krishna teaches in the Gita is a reply to this moment.

Arjuna's reasoning: what is a kingdom worth if the people he would share it with lie dead? Govinda, one of Krishna's names, is often explained as "protector of cows," recalling his youth among the cowherds of Vraja. Arjuna's grief is sincere, and much of the Gita is Krishna's long, patient reply to it.

Arjuna's objection is a serious one. The Kauravas he would have to kill are his own cousins: their father, Dhritarashtra, and Arjuna's father, Pandu, were brothers. No kingdom, he argues, could bring happiness bought with their deaths, so refusing to fight looks to him like the right choice. Krishna will soon call it faint-heartedness born of grief, and the Gita answers it at length. Madhava is another of Krishna's names.

Arjuna has said that the Kauravas, blinded by greed, see no wrong in destroying a family. Now he turns the same charge on his own side: they too are about to do a great wrong for the pleasures of a kingdom. Chapter 1 is traditionally titled Arjuna Vishada Yoga, "the yoga of Arjuna's despondency."

Arjuna would rather die unarmed than fight his own family. In the next verse, the last of chapter 1, he sinks down in the chariot, casts aside his bow and arrows, his mind overcome with grief. The scene is set: a celebrated warrior, frozen by doubt between two armies.

Chapter 2 opens with Arjuna in tears. Krishna, called "the Blessed Lord" (Bhagavan) throughout the Gita, answers sharply: this despondency is unworthy of him. The tone will soon soften, but first Krishna tries to shake his friend awake.

Krishna's first demand is blunt: shake off this weakness of heart and stand up. Parantapa, "scorcher of foes," is one of Arjuna's many epithets. Swami Vivekananda said the whole message of the Gita lies embedded in this one verse, which he read as a call to strength and fearlessness.

Arjuna answers Krishna's rebuke with a question that shows where his hesitation comes from: reverence. Facing him across the field are Bhishma, the revered grandsire of both families, and Drona, who taught the princes of both sides the art of war. How can he shoot arrows at the very people he owes the most honour? Madhusudana, "slayer of the demon Madhu," is one of Krishna's many names.

Arjuna would rather live on alms, a life thought unfitting for a warrior prince, than kill his elders and enjoy a kingdom stained with their blood. Guru here means revered elders and teachers such as Bhishma and Drona. In the verses that follow, he admits he no longer knows what is right.

This is the turning point of the whole Gita. Arjuna admits he no longer knows what dharma, right duty, requires, and asks Krishna to teach him as a disciple. From here on, a conversation between friends becomes a teaching from guru to student.

Arjuna has told Krishna "I will not fight!" and fallen silent. Krishna, smiling, begins his teaching here: Arjuna speaks words of wisdom, yet grieves for what the wise do not grieve over. The next verses explain why: the real self of each person, the atman, does not die with the body.

Krishna's first argument is that the self has no beginning and no end. Schools read his "we" differently. Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita) sees here many eternal selves, distinct from one another and from God; Shankara (Advaita) says the plural refers to bodies, and that in the highest truth there is one Self.

Krishna continues his answer to Arjuna's grief. The self, the "dweller in the body" (dehi), passes through childhood, youth and old age while remaining the same self, and in the same way it passes on to another body at death. The point is that death is one more change of the kind we already live through, not an ending. Dhira, "the steadfast one," is someone whose understanding holds firm through all of them.

Krishna's practical advice: heat and cold, pleasure and pain all come and go, so bear them patiently. Matra-sparsha, "contacts of matter," means the meeting of the senses with their objects, where these feelings arise. Because they never last, they need not shake a person, a first step toward the evenness of mind the chapter goes on to teach. Titiksha, this patient endurance, became one of the classic virtues of a seeker in Advaita Vedanta.

Krishna states the principle behind his consolation: what is unreal never truly is, and what is real never ceases to be. Sat is what truly is and does not change; asat is what has no lasting being. In context he applies it to the self, which endures, and the body, which does not. Shankara's Advaita reads sat and asat as Brahman, the one reality, and the passing world of appearances; Ramanuja reads them as the eternal self and the perishable body.

The body comes to an end; the one who dwells in it does not. From this Krishna draws a conclusion for Arjuna: fight. Shankara comments that the words are not a command to make war but the removal of the grief and confusion holding Arjuna back from a duty he had already taken up.

The self is not a killer and cannot be killed: Krishna's answer to Arjuna's dread of slaying his elders. Ralph Waldo Emerson's poem "Brahma" opens with the same thought, drawing on this verse or its near-twin in the Katha Upanishad: "If the red slayer think he slays, / Or if the slain think he is slain."

Perhaps the Gita's most famous statement about the atman, the true self: it is never born and never dies, and it is not killed when the body is. For Arjuna, dreading the deaths of his elders, this is the heart of Krishna's consolation: the true self of the people he grieves for cannot be destroyed. This verse and the one before closely match two verses of the Katha Upanishad, where Yama, the lord of death, teaches the boy Nachiketa what survives death.

One of the best-loved images in the Gita: the body as clothing, worn out and exchanged for new. Krishna's point to the grieving Arjuna is that death is a change of garment, not the end of the one who wears it. Belief in rebirth (punarjanma) is shared by Hindu, Buddhist, Jain and Sikh traditions, though they describe what passes from life to life very differently.

Weapons, fire, water, wind: none of the forces that destroy a body can touch the self. Krishna says this on a battlefield, with weapons all around. Verses from this passage are often recited at Hindu funerals and memorials.

Krishna turns from philosophy to plain realism: what is born will die, and in the Gita's view, what dies will be born again. If something cannot be avoided, grief cannot change it. Arjuna is mourning people who are still alive; Krishna asks him to see the whole cycle.

Krishna gives Arjuna another reason not to grieve. Beings come from the unmanifest (avyakta), what cannot be perceived, appear for a while, and return to it at death. A life is only the visible middle of a longer story, so lamenting its end mistakes the part for the whole. Avyakta becomes an important word later in the Gita, especially in chapters 8 and 12.

Krishna sums up the first part of his answer where it began, with grief. The dehi, the self that dwells in every body, can never be slain, so, Krishna says, there is no cause to grieve for any creature. The word Besant translates "invulnerable," avadhya, means literally "not to be killed."

Krishna turns from the eternal self to svadharma, one's own duty. For Arjuna, a prince of the kshatriya (warrior) class, that means fighting a righteous war. Readings of passages like this range from literal to allegorical: Gandhi read the battle as an image of the struggle between good and evil within each person.

Krishna tells Arjuna to fight holding pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat as equal, and says that acting this way he will incur no sin. The argument has moved from duty to inner attitude: commentators explain that what binds is not the act alone but acting from craving for a particular result. This evenness of mind is the seed of what the Gita calls yoga, here a discipline of action rather than physical postures.

Krishna has just turned from knowledge of the self to yoga, which here means acting with steady understanding. Of this path he promises that no effort is wasted and no adverse result follows (pratyavaya, Besant's "transgression"); even a little protects. He returns to the idea in chapter 6, when Arjuna asks what becomes of someone who tries and falls short.

Krishna contrasts two kinds of mind. Resolute understanding (vyavasayatmika buddhi) is single and focused; the thoughts of the irresolute branch out endlessly. The point is that steady action needs one clear aim, while a mind pulled by many wants never settles. In the next verses Krishna applies this to people chasing the many rewards promised by ritual. The one-pointed mind (ekagrata) becomes a central ideal in Indian meditation traditions.

Perhaps the most quoted verse of the Gita and the heart of karma yoga, the path of action. It has four parts: a right to action, no claim on its results, no acting for the sake of results, and no retreat into inaction. Gandhi named his Gujarati translation of the Gita Anasaktiyoga, "the yoga of non-attachment."

One of the Gita's best-known definitions of yoga, often quoted in Sanskrit as yogah karmasu kaushalam. The skill meant here is acting without being bound by results, so that neither good nor bad deeds tie one down. Buddhi, Besant's "Pure Reason," is the discerning intellect.

Earlier in this chapter Krishna warned against those who prize the letter of the Vedas for the heavenly rewards their rituals promise. Besant's "bewildered by the Scriptures" renders a phrase often read as a mind pulled this way and that by all it has heard. When it stands still in samadhi, deep contemplation, that is yoga.

Arjuna asks a practical question: what is a person of steady wisdom, a sthitaprajna, actually like? How do they speak, sit and walk? Krishna's answer fills the rest of chapter 2, and Gandhi had these closing verses recited at the daily prayers of his ashram.

The first mark of the sthitaprajna: one who has let go of every craving of the mind and is content in the self alone. The happiness described comes from within, not from getting what one wants. Besant capitalises "Self" for the deeper self, the atman, as distinct from the everyday self.

Krishna continues his portrait of the person of steady wisdom. Such a sage (muni) is not shaken by sorrow, does not crave pleasure, and is free of passion, fear and anger. The point is a mind whose balance no longer depends on how things turn out. The same three, raga, bhaya and krodha, appear together again in chapter 4. Muni is traditionally linked with mauna, contemplative silence.

Another mark of the sthitaprajna, the person of steady wisdom: meeting fair fortune and foul alike, neither rejoicing at the one nor resenting the other. The verse's closing words, "the understanding is well poised" (prajna pratishthita), recur through this passage like a refrain.

A memorable image: the tortoise drawing in its limbs. The sthitaprajna can withdraw the senses from their objects at will, as a tortoise pulls in head and feet. Many teachers point out that a tortoise can also put them out again: the image is of mastery, not suppression.

Krishna is frank about how hard this is: even a wise person who is striving can be carried off by the senses. Pramathini, the word for the senses here, suggests something turbulent and violent. Arjuna makes the same complaint about the mind in chapter 6.

posts.display: Man, musing on the objects of sense, conceiveth an attachment to these; from attachment ariseth desire; from desire anger cometh forth.
posts.caption: One of the Gita's best-known passages traces a chain of cause and effect in the mind. It starts not with an action but with mere dwelling on objects of the senses, which breeds attachment, then desire, and then, when desire is thwarted, anger. The next verse completes the chain.

In the verse before this, Krishna traced how dwelling on the objects of the senses breeds attachment, then desire, then anger. Here the chain runs on downward: anger brings confusion, memory of what one has learned slips away, the discerning intellect (buddhi) is lost, and the person is ruined. The verses that follow describe the way back.

After the downward chain from desire to ruin, Krishna describes the way back. Raga and dvesha, attraction and aversion, drive that chain; free of them, the senses can move among their objects without dragging the mind along. Prasada, the calm clarity this brings, is what Besant translates as "peace."

Without inner harmony, there is no clear understanding and no steady contemplation, and without these, no peace. The verse ends with a question that answers itself. Ayukta, "unharmonised," is the opposite of yukta, one joined in yoga.

Another image from everyday life: a ship driven off course by a gale. When the mind follows whichever sense is roaming, understanding is carried off the same way. The word for understanding here, prajna, is the one in sthitaprajna, "of steady wisdom."

A famous paradox. What the world is awake to, the sage treats as night, and what the world sleeps through, the sage is awake to. Commentators often read it as two kinds of attention: one alert to worldly pursuits, the other to the self. Samyami means one who is self-controlled.

Rivers pour into the ocean all year, yet it stays full and unmoved within its shores. Krishna uses the image for a person whose peace does not depend on satisfying each desire. The contrast at the end is pointed: kama-kami, "one who desires desires," does not find that peace.

The description of the steady sage closes simply: no cravings, no sense of "mine" (nirmama), no ego-sense (nirahankara). In the Gita's teaching, peace (shanti) comes not from getting what one wants but from letting go of "I" and "mine." Ahankara, literally "I-maker," is the sense of being a separate doer, a key idea in later chapters.

Chapter 2 ends by naming the steady wisdom it has described: brahmi sthiti, the state of Brahman. Whoever reaches it is no longer bewildered, and whoever holds to it even at the hour of death reaches brahma-nirvana, the peace of Brahman. Nirvana, literally "blowing out," is better known from Buddhism. That completes Arjuna's crisis and Krishna's first teaching. Thank you for reading along.
